In colonial Williamsburg, I saw a presentation on the legal system circa 1770 in Virginia. At the time, they considered depriving a person of freedom was "cruel and unusual", and the only time you'd spend in jail was a maximum of 3 months awaiting your trial (often only a couple weeks). The punishment ranged from a fine (not attending church) to hanging (murder, horse theft). Most major crimes like thievery were punished by branding (you'd get a big T branded into your hand). The punishment was social stigma. Imagine if we punished pot smokers by branding a big pot leaf into their hand instead of sending them to prison for a couple years.

I'm not saying that legal system was better, but our idea of "rehabilitation" where we send people out with the complete inability to get anything but minimum wage jobs thanks to background checks, while simultaneously giving them gang connections -- and paying 50k/year of taxpayer money to do it -- is that really working?

Other fun notes from collonial Williamsburg law: All men were required to own a gun unless they had a special permit not to (Quakers, mostly). It was illegal not to have a gun. Also, husbands would be responsible for most crimes their wives committed.
